results.evidence: Section 11.3: "The limitations in Sections 11.1 and 11.2 do not apply to: (a) a party's fraud, gross negligence or willful misconduct; (b) Customer's obligation to pay fees due under this Agreement; or (c) Customer's obligations under Section 10.2." Read with Section 10.2: "...including claims for bodily injury, death or property damage occurring at any event at which Rental Inventory is used, regardless of whether caused in part by Provider's installation or handling of the Rental Inventory."
results.reason: Section 11.3(c) carves only Customer's Section 10.2 indemnity out of the cap and the consequential-damages exclusion. That indemnity is broad: it covers all claims relating to Rental Inventory, including injuries caused in part by Provider's installation. Provider's Section 10.1 indemnity, which covers its own negligence and vehicle accidents, stays capped at 12 months of fees under 11.1. The result is that Nonaisk has unlimited exposure, including for Zouduth's negligent setup, while Zouduth's exposure is limited. Ordinary negligence by Zouduth falls outside the 11.3(a) gross-negligence carve-out. The term sheet called for mutual limitations and negligence-based indemnities (8.2, 8.3), but Section 17.4 supersedes it. No other document cures the imbalance. The agreement is newly signed and no claim has arisen, so the issue can still be raised, for example as an amendment under Section 17.5 or as risk advice to the client.

results.evidence: DPA §12.1: "This DPA and all disputes arising out of or relating to it, including disputes concerning the Processing of Customer Data or any Security Incident, are governed by the laws of the State of New York, without regard to its conflict of laws principles." DPA §12.2: "Each party irrevocably submits to the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts of New York County, New York..." By contrast, MSA §16.1–16.2 choose Delaware law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts in Wilmington, Delaware.
results.reason: The two documents set conflicting exclusive forums and governing laws. The precedence clause in MSA §2.3 does not fix this. It makes the DPA prevail for Personal Data matters, so New York law and forum govern data disputes while Delaware governs everything else. A single Security Incident could therefore be split across both forums. For example, a claim under DPA §6.4 for breach costs would go to New York. A related claim for negligence or violation of law, or an argument about the liability cap under MSA §§10, 11 and 16, would go to Delaware. DPA §11 itself reaches back into the Delaware-governed MSA §11, which makes the split more likely. Nonaisk, as Customer, would be the party pursuing breach claims and would bear the cost of parallel litigation and the risk of inconsistent results. Nothing in the folder shows this was intended or accepted: the term sheet calls for Delaware law and forum only. The DPA's signature blocks are blank, and the MSA and DPA can still be amended by a signed writing (MSA §17.5, DPA §13.2). The problem is therefore still actionable.

results.evidence: DPA Section 1.3: "'Customer Data' means Personal Data uploaded by Customer to the Zouduth Dispatch Platform in connection with the Services, including order records, Event Client names and delivery addresses that Customer enters or imports into the Dispatch Platform." Compare MSA Section 1.4: "'Customer Data' means all data Provider receives from or collects for Customer in performing Services ... also includes venue access information, delivery sign-offs, and any data entered into or generated by the Dispatch Platform."
results.reason: The DPA's definition of Customer Data covers only Personal Data that Customer itself uploads to the Dispatch Platform. The MSA definition is broader and includes data Provider collects for Customer, such as on-site sign-offs, venue access codes and paper records collected by crews. Under MSA 2.3 the DPA prevails on Personal Data matters. As a result, crew-collected personal data falls outside the DPA's protections: the 48-hour breach notice (6.1), subprocessor controls (Section 5), and return and deletion (Section 8). The term sheet (6.1) shows the parties intended to cover crew-collected data, so the narrowing is not a deliberate concession. Nothing in the folder fixes the gap. This hurts Nonaisk, which as controller bears the notification and compliance duties. The DPA is newly signed and can be amended under DPA 13.2 and MSA 17.5, so the issue is still actionable.

results.evidence: Section 15.2: "Provider may assign this Agreement, in whole or in part, without Customer's consent, to any Affiliate or to any successor to all or substantially all of Provider's business or assets to which this Agreement relates, whether by merger, sale of stock, sale of assets or otherwise." Section 15.1, by contrast: "Customer may not assign or transfer this Agreement, in whole or in part, without Provider's prior written consent."
results.reason: Section 15.2 lets Zouduth assign without Nonaisk's consent to any Affiliate or successor. It does not exclude Competitors, even though the MSA defines "Competitor" in Section 1.2 and never uses that term anywhere. This departs from the agreed term in term sheet Section 7.1: "Neither party may assign without consent, except to a successor that is not a Competitor." Section 17.4 of the MSA supersedes the term sheet, and the term sheet's assignment terms were non-binding in any event (term sheet Section 12.1), so Nonaisk cannot fall back on them. Nonaisk's only protection is after-the-fact notice within 30 days. A rival rental company, or its logistics affiliate, could therefore take over the contract. The confidentiality and data restrictions bind "Provider" and its "successors and assigns" (Section 15.3), so they would pass to the assignee. That assignee would then hold Nonaisk's Customer Data, Event Client lists and pricing. Nonaisk would also remain bound to the $1.85M Annual Minimum and could not terminate the agreement over the assignment. Nothing in the folder cures or waives this. The agreement is in its first year and the terms can still be addressed by amendment, so the problem is still actionable.
